Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function sat_add(a, b, bits) implementing saturating signed two's-complement addition.

Contract:
- bits defines the representable range [-(2**(bits-1)), 2**(bits-1) - 1].
- All three arguments must be ints and must NOT be bools (note: isinstance(True, int) is True in Python; bools must still be rejected). If any argument is a bool or not an int, raise ValueError.
- If bits < 1, raise ValueError.
- If a or b is itself outside the representable range for bits, raise ValueError (the inputs must already be representable; only the SUM saturates).
- Otherwise return a + b clamped (saturated) into the representable range.
- bits == 1 is valid: the representable range is [-1, 0].

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function div_round_half_away(num, den) that returns the integer nearest to the exact rational value num/den, with ties rounded away from zero.

Contract:
- Both arguments must be ints and must NOT be bools; otherwise raise ValueError.
- If den == 0, raise ValueError.
- Rounding: return the nearest integer to num/den. When num/den is exactly halfway between two integers, round AWAY from zero (e.g. 7/2 -> 4, -7/2 -> -4).
- The sign of the result follows the mathematical sign of num/den; den may be negative (7 over -2 -> -4).
- The result must be EXACT for arbitrarily large integers (magnitudes around 10**30 are tested); converting to float loses precision at that scale, so the computation must stay in integer arithmetic.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function add_months(year, month, day, n) that adds n calendar months to a proleptic Gregorian date and returns a tuple (year, month, day).

Contract:
- All four arguments must be ints and must NOT be bools; otherwise raise ValueError.
- The input date must be valid, else raise ValueError: year >= 1, 1 <= month <= 12, and 1 <= day <= number of days in that month of that year.
- Leap-year rule (applied to ALL years, proleptic Gregorian): divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, unless also divisible by 400.
- n may be negative, zero, or large; month arithmetic carries into the year in both directions.
- Day clamping: if the original day-of-month does not exist in the target month, clamp DOWN to the last day of the target month (e.g. January 31 plus 1 month lands on February 28 or 29). Never overflow into the following month.
- If the resulting year would be < 1, raise ValueError.
- Must work for years far beyond 9999 (e.g. year 999999), so the datetime module's year range is insufficient.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function bucket_counts(values, edges) that histograms integer values into buckets defined by an edge list, with mixed boundary semantics.

Contract:
- edges must be a list of at least 2 non-bool ints in strictly increasing order; otherwise raise ValueError. values must be a list of non-bool ints; otherwise raise ValueError.
- n edges define n-1 buckets. For every bucket EXCEPT the last, bucket i covers the half-open range [edges[i], edges[i+1]). The LAST bucket is closed on BOTH ends: [edges[-2], edges[-1]].
- Consequence: a value equal to an interior edge counts in the bucket to its RIGHT; a value equal to edges[-1] counts in the last bucket.
- Any value < edges[0] or > edges[-1] raises ValueError.
- Return a list of counts of length len(edges) - 1. An empty values list yields all zeros.
- Neither input list may be mutated (in particular, do not sort values in place).

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function edit(commands) that simulates a one-line text editor and returns the final state as a tuple (text, cursor).

The buffer starts empty and the cursor starts at position 0 (the cursor sits between characters; position k means k characters are to its left).

commands is a list of strings, processed left to right:
- "type <text>": insert <text> at the cursor; the cursor ends immediately after the inserted text. <text> is everything after the first space and may itself contain further spaces; it must be non-empty.
- "left <n>" / "right <n>": move the cursor n positions, clamping at 0 and at the end of the buffer. Clamping is not an error.
- "backspace <n>": delete up to n characters immediately before the cursor (fewer if the cursor has fewer than n characters to its left); the cursor moves left by the number of characters actually deleted.
- "undo": revert the most recent not-yet-undone command that actually changed the buffer, restoring BOTH the buffer AND the cursor to their values from immediately before that command (cursor motion performed after that command is discarded). A backspace that deleted zero characters did not change the buffer and is never an undo target. "undo" when nothing is undoable is a no-op. Undo itself can never be undone.

Raise ValueError for a malformed command at the moment it is processed:
- unknown verb, or a verb with no argument (e.g. "left" alone, "type" alone);
- "type" with an empty payload ("type " with nothing after the space);
- left/right/backspace whose argument is not a non-empty string of ASCII digits ("-2", "+3", "2x", "2 3", and "" are all malformed) or whose numeric value is 0;
- "undo" followed by anything (e.g. "undo 2").

The input list must not be mutated. Return the result as a tuple (text, cursor).

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function decode_frame(frame) that validates and decodes a hex-encoded protocol frame and returns the payload as a list of ints.

frame is a string of hex characters (case-insensitive), encoding a byte sequence two characters per byte: a header byte, a length byte N, N payload bytes, and a final checksum byte. A frame is valid when:
- the header byte equals 0xA5;
- the total number of bytes is exactly 3 + N;
- (header + N + sum(payload bytes) + checksum) is divisible by 256.

Validation must be performed in exactly this order, raising ValueError with exactly these messages; only the first applicable error is raised:
1. the string has an odd number of characters -> ValueError("odd length")
2. any character is not a hex digit (0-9, a-f, A-F) -> ValueError("not hex")
3. the string has fewer than 6 characters -> ValueError("truncated")
4. the header byte is not 0xA5 -> ValueError("bad header")
5. the total byte count differs from 3 + N (too short OR too long) -> ValueError("length mismatch")
6. the checksum equation fails -> ValueError("bad checksum")

So a string that is both odd-length and contains non-hex characters must raise "odd length", and a 2-character non-hex string must raise "not hex", not "truncated". An empty payload (N = 0) is legal: the minimum valid frame is 6 characters. Return the payload byte values as a list of ints (empty list for N = 0).

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function outline_paths(lines) that converts an indentation-based outline into the list of leaf paths.

lines is a list of strings. Lines that are empty or contain only whitespace (spaces and/or tabs) are skipped entirely and never participate in validation or level tracking. For every other line: the leading whitespace determines the node's level, and the rest of the line, with trailing whitespace stripped, is the node's name (interior spaces in names are preserved).

Rules, checked per line in this exact order, processing lines top to bottom and raising on the first violation:
1. If the leading whitespace contains a tab character -> ValueError("tab in indent").
2. If the number of leading spaces is not a multiple of 2 -> ValueError("odd indent"). Level = leading spaces / 2.
3. The first non-blank line must be at level 0, and each non-blank line may be at most one level deeper than the previous non-blank line (any decrease is fine). Violations -> ValueError("indent jump"). Note this means an indented first line raises "indent jump".
4. If the name contains "/" -> ValueError("slash in name").

A node at level L is a child of the nearest preceding node at level L-1. Multiple level-0 roots are allowed (the outline is a forest). A leaf is a node with no children. Return the leaf paths (names joined with "/", from root to leaf) in the order the leaves appear in the input. Return [] for an empty or all-blank input. The input list must not be mutated.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function untilde(s) that decodes a tilde-escaped string and returns the decoded str.

Scan s left to right. "~" introduces an escape sequence (case-sensitive):
- "~~" decodes to a literal "~"
- "~n" decodes to a newline (U+000A)
- "~t" decodes to a tab (U+0009)
- "~xHH" decodes to the character with code point 0xHH, where HH is exactly two hex digits (0-9, a-f, A-F; either case). Exactly two characters are consumed after "~x", so "~x123" decodes to chr(0x12) followed by the literal "3".

Errors (ValueError with exactly these messages). The scan proceeds left to right and the FIRST error encountered by position wins:
- "~" as the last character with nothing after it -> ValueError("dangling escape")
- "~" followed by any character other than "~", "n", "t", "x" -> ValueError("bad escape"). Uppercase "~N", "~T", "~X" are bad escapes.
- "~x" followed by fewer than two remaining characters, or where either of the next two characters is not a hex digit -> ValueError("bad hex")
- any literal (unescaped) character in the input with code point < 32 -> ValueError("raw control"). Escape sequences may still PRODUCE such characters in the output ("~x00" and "~n" are fine); only raw occurrences in the input are forbidden.

So an input consisting of "a", a real newline, then "~" raises "raw control" (the newline at position 1 precedes the dangling "~"), while "~q" followed by a real newline raises "bad escape". The empty string decodes to "".

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function apportion(weights, total) that splits an integer total into integer shares proportional to weights, using the largest-remainder method.

Contract:
- weights must be a non-empty list of non-bool ints, each >= 0, with at least one positive entry; total must be a non-bool int >= 0. Any violation raises ValueError.
- Let the total of all weights. Entry i's exact quota is weights[i] * total / s. Each share starts at the floor of its quota, computed EXACTLY with integer arithmetic as (weights[i] * total) // s (no floats).
- Let r = total minus the sum of those floors. Give exactly one extra unit to each of the r entries with the LARGEST remainder (weights[i] * total) % s. Break remainder ties by LOWER index first.
- The returned list must sum to exactly total and have the same length as weights.
- The input list must NOT be mutated.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function format_duration(seconds) that formats a signed integer number of seconds as a clock-style string.

Contract:
- seconds must be an int and must NOT be a bool; otherwise raise ValueError.
- Let the magnitude of seconds. All time components are computed from a (truncation toward zero; components are never negative).
- If a < 3600, the format is "M:SS": total minutes a // 60 WITHOUT zero-padding (may be a bare 0), then seconds zero-padded to exactly 2 digits.
- If a >= 3600, the format is "H:MM:SS": hours WITHOUT zero-padding (no upper bound; hours may have any number of digits), then minutes and seconds each zero-padded to exactly 2 digits.
- The threshold is exact: a == 3600 must use the "H:MM:SS" form.
- If seconds < 0, prefix a single "-" before the formatted value.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function decode_varints(data) that decodes a byte stream of zigzag-encoded base-128 varints and returns a list of signed ints.

data is a list of byte values. First validate every element: each must be an int with 0 <= value <= 255; booleans must be rejected even though bool subclasses int. Any bad element raises ValueError("bad byte") before any decoding is attempted (so [0x80, 300] raises "bad byte", not a decoding error).

Then decode the stream as consecutive varints. Each varint is one or more bytes: each byte contributes its low 7 bits, least-significant group first; a set high bit (0x80) means another byte follows; a clear high bit ends the varint. After assembling the unsigned value u, zigzag-decode it to a signed value: even u decodes to u // 2, odd u decodes to -((u + 1) // 2). (So unsigned 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 decode to 0, -1, 1, -2, 2.)

Decoding errors (ValueError with exactly these messages):
- a varint whose first 5 bytes all have the continuation bit set raises ValueError("too long"); this takes precedence even when the stream also ends there (e.g. [0x80]*5 is "too long", not truncated);
- the stream ends while a varint of fewer than 5 bytes still has its continuation bit set -> ValueError("truncated");
- a non-canonical (overlong) encoding, i.e. a varint of 2 or more bytes whose final byte is 0x00, must raise ValueError with the exact message 'overlong' (e.g. [0x80, 0x00], which encodes 0 in two bytes).

A varint of exactly 5 bytes whose 5th byte lacks the continuation bit is legal. The input list must not be mutated. Return [] for an empty stream.

Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function wrap_text(s, width) that greedily wraps text into lines and returns them as a list of strings. Words are maximal runs of non-whitespace characters; any run of whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) separates words and is never preserved. width must be an int and must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad width'). Greedy packing: words are placed on the current line joined by single spaces as long as the line stays within width characters; a word that does not fit starts a new line. A word longer than width is handled specially: the current line (if any) is finished first, then the word is cut into consecutive pieces of exactly width characters, each full piece becoming its own line, and the final remainder (between 1 and width characters) starts a new current line that later words may still join. Returned lines never have leading or trailing spaces and are never empty. An empty or all-whitespace input returns []. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function split_identifier(s) that splits a programming identifier into its constituent words and returns them as a list of strings preserving original case. Allowed characters are ASCII letters, ASCII digits, and underscores; any other character (including non-ASCII letters) -> ValueError('bad char'). Underscores are pure separators: they are removed, runs of underscores act as one separator, and leading or trailing underscores produce no words. Within a run of letters and digits, words break at every letter-digit or digit-letter boundary and at every lowercase-to-uppercase boundary. A run of two or more consecutive uppercase letters is an acronym: if it is immediately followed by a lowercase letter, the LAST uppercase letter belongs to the following word (so an acronym then a capitalized word split before that final capital). A single uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters forms one capitalized word. Digit runs are whole words. An empty input (or one that is only underscores) returns []. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function expand_tabs(s, stop) that expands tab characters into spaces using tab stops every `stop` columns and returns the resulting string. stop must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad stop'). Column arithmetic: the column starts at 0; every character other than tab and newline advances the column by exactly 1 and is copied through unchanged. A tab is replaced by however many spaces are needed to reach the NEXT multiple of stop; a tab sitting exactly on a multiple of stop still advances a full stop (it never produces zero spaces). A newline is copied through and resets the column to 0. Carriage returns and all other control characters are ordinary one-column characters. The empty string returns ''. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function interval_subtract(a, b) computing the difference of two closed INTEGER interval lists. Each list contains [start, end] pairs of ints; both lists are already sorted by start and internally disjoint. Before any computation, every interval in BOTH lists must satisfy start <= end; any violation -> ValueError('bad interval'). Semantics are integer semantics on closed intervals: the result covers exactly the integers covered by some interval of a but by no interval of b, expressed as the sorted list of maximal closed intervals [start, end] (a single surviving integer x appears as [x, x]). For example removing [3,5] from [1,10] leaves [1,2] and [6,10]. One b interval may bite several a intervals and vice versa. Touching matters: removing [5,9] from [1,5] leaves [1,4]. Empty a returns []; empty b returns the intervals of a unchanged in value. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function rect_overlap(r1, r2) returning the area of the intersection of two axis-aligned rectangles as an int. Each rectangle must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly 4 values (x1, y1, x2, y2); each value must be an int and must not be a bool; and it must satisfy x1 <= x2 and y1 <= y2. Any violation of any of these -> ValueError('bad rect'). (x1, y1) is one corner and (x2, y2) the opposite corner; coordinates may be negative. Degenerate rectangles with zero width or height are VALID inputs and simply have zero area. Rectangles that only touch along an edge or at a corner overlap with area 0, not an error. Return the exact integer overlap area, 0 whenever the interiors do not intersect. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function count_covered(intervals) returning how many distinct INTEGERS are covered by a list of closed integer intervals. intervals is a list of [start, end] pairs in ARBITRARY order that may overlap, nest, duplicate, or touch. Every bound must be an int and must not be a bool, and every interval must satisfy start <= end; any violation -> ValueError('bad interval'). Counting is over integers, not length: [1, 3] covers the three integers 1, 2, 3, and the adjacent pair [1, 2] plus [3, 4] covers four integers in total. Overlapping regions count once ([1, 3] with [2, 5] covers five). The input list must NOT be mutated: do not sort it in place and do not reorder its elements. Bounds may be negative. An empty list returns 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function turtle(prog) that runs a turtle-graphics command string and returns the final state as a tuple (x, y, heading). The turtle starts at (0, 0) heading 'N'; headings are the letters N, E, S, W with x growing east and y growing north. Commands are single characters: 'F' moves one step in the current heading, 'B' moves one step backward WITHOUT changing heading, 'L' and 'R' rotate 90 degrees left/right. A command may be prefixed by a repetition count: one or more ASCII digits meaning the command repeats that many times ('12F' moves forward twelve). A count whose first digit is '0' -> ValueError('bad count'). A run of digits at the very end of the program with no command after it -> ValueError('dangling count'). Any character that is not a digit and not one of F, B, L, R -> ValueError('bad command'). Errors are detected left to right as the program is scanned. The empty program returns (0, 0, 'N'). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function grant_requests(capacity, events) simulating a token-bucket rate limiter and returning a list of bools, one per event, True when the request was granted. capacity must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1 -> otherwise ValueError('bad capacity'). events is a list; each event must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly two values (timestamp, amount), both ints and neither a bool, with amount at least 1; any violation -> ValueError('bad event'). Timestamps must be non-decreasing across the list; a timestamp smaller than its predecessor -> ValueError('time warp'). Events are validated and processed strictly in list order, so a malformed event is only reported when reached. Bucket semantics: the bucket holds `capacity` tokens and is FULL before the first event. Between consecutive events it refills by 1 token per unit of elapsed timestamp difference, capped at capacity; the refill is applied before judging the request at that timestamp, and two events with equal timestamps get no refill between them. A request is granted iff the bucket then holds at least `amount` tokens, and a granted request removes `amount` tokens; a denied request removes nothing. An amount larger than capacity is a legal request that is simply always denied. An empty events list returns []. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function stopwatch(events) simulating a stopwatch and returning a tuple (total, laps). events is a list of (timestamp, op) items processed in order. Each item must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly two values, the timestamp an int and not a bool, and the op one of the strings 'start', 'stop', 'lap', 'reset'; any violation -> ValueError('bad event'). Timestamps must be STRICTLY increasing across the whole list; an equal or smaller timestamp -> ValueError('time warp'). The stopwatch begins stopped with an accumulated total of 0 and no laps. 'start' while already running -> ValueError('already running'); otherwise it marks the segment start. 'stop' while not running -> ValueError('not running'); otherwise it adds the elapsed segment time to the accumulated total. 'lap' while not running -> ValueError('not running'); while running it records the CURRENT total elapsed time (accumulated completed segments plus the running segment so far) into the laps list. 'reset' while running -> ValueError('still running'); while stopped it zeroes the accumulated total AND clears the laps list. Return (total, laps) where total counts only COMPLETED segments: a segment still running when the list ends contributes nothing. An empty list returns (0, []). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function matrix_shape(m) that validates a rectangular numeric matrix and returns its shape as a tuple (rows, columns). Checks run in a fixed order and only the FIRST failure is reported, each as a ValueError with exactly the given message. First: m must be a list -> 'not a list'; then m must be non-empty -> 'empty'. Then rows are examined strictly top to bottom, and for each row in this order: the row must be a list -> 'row not list'; the row must be non-empty -> 'empty row'; the row's length must equal the first row's length -> 'ragged'; then the row's cells are scanned left to right and each must be an int or a float but never a bool -> 'bad cell'. Note the ordering consequences: a bad cell in row 1 is reported even when row 2 is ragged, but a row's own length check fires before that same row's cells are scanned. Return (number of rows, number of columns) after all checks pass. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function parse_money(s) that parses a strictly formatted decimal money amount and returns the value as an integer number of cents. Grammar: an optional single leading '-' (no '+'), then the integer part, then optionally a '.' followed by EXACTLY two digits. The integer part is either plain digits with no separators and no leading zero (except exactly '0' by itself), or comma-grouped: a first group of 1 to 3 digits not starting with '0', followed by one or more groups of exactly 3 digits each preceded by a comma. Mixing is not allowed: once commas appear, every group after the first must be exactly 3 digits. Anything violating the grammar -> ValueError('bad amount'): that includes '.50' (missing integer part), '1.5' (one decimal digit), '1.505' (three), '007', '0,123', '12,34', '1,2345', '+1', whitespace anywhere, and the empty string. A minus sign with a zero value is legal input and the function then returns 0 (so '-0.00' gives 0). Examples: '1,234.56' gives 123456; '-12' gives -1200; '0.99' gives 99. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function cron_field(field, lo, hi) that expands one cron-style field string into the sorted deduplicated list of matching integers within the inclusive bounds [lo, hi]. lo and hi must both be ints and not bools with lo <= hi; otherwise -> ValueError('bad bounds'). The field is a comma-separated list of items with no whitespace anywhere. Each item is one of: '*' (every value from lo to hi); '*/K' (lo, lo+K, lo+2K, ... up to hi); 'N' (a single value); 'N-M' (every value from N to M inclusive); or 'N-M/K' (N, N+K, ... up to M). N, M, K are unsigned decimal digit runs; leading zeros are ALLOWED and carry no meaning. A step on a bare single value (an item shaped like 'N/K') is invalid syntax. Error taxonomy, each a ValueError with exactly the message: any syntactically malformed item (empty item, empty field, missing digits, signs, stray characters, a step attached to a bare value) -> 'bad field'; a range with N greater than M -> 'bad range'; an N or M outside [lo, hi] -> 'out of range'; a step K equal to 0 -> 'bad step'. Duplicates across items are fine and collapse in the sorted output. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function to_base(n, base) that renders an integer in an arbitrary base and returns the string. base must be an int, must not be a bool, and must satisfy 2 <= base <= 36; otherwise -> ValueError('bad base'). n must be an int and must not be a bool; otherwise -> ValueError('bad number'). Digits above 9 use the lowercase letters a through z, so base 16 uses 0-9 then a-f. The value zero always renders as the single character 0. A negative number renders as a single leading minus sign followed by the rendering of its absolute value. The result never carries redundant leading zeros (other than the lone 0 for zero itself) and never carries a plus sign. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function from_base(s, base) that parses a string of digits in an arbitrary base and returns the integer value. base must be an int, must not be a bool, and must satisfy 2 <= base <= 36; otherwise -> ValueError('bad base'). s must be a str. Parsing is case insensitive: digits above 9 are the letters a through z (or A through Z) with a meaning 10 up to z meaning 35. An optional single leading minus sign is allowed and negates the value; no plus sign is allowed. Leading zeros are permitted and carry no meaning. Any of the following -> ValueError('bad digits'): an empty string, a string that is only the minus sign, a character that is not a valid digit for the given base, a digit whose value is not strictly less than base, and any whitespace. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function to_roman(n) that renders a positive integer as an uppercase Roman numeral string in strict subtractive form. n must be an int, must not be a bool, and must satisfy 1 <= n <= 3999; otherwise -> ValueError('out of range'). Use the standard symbols where I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500, M is 1000, and the six subtractive compounds IV is 4, IX is 9, XL is 40, XC is 90, CD is 400, CM is 900. Greedily emit the largest value that fits, so 1994 renders as MCMXCIV and 58 as LVIII. A symbol is never repeated four times in a row because the subtractive compounds are used instead. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function col_label(n) that converts a positive column index into its spreadsheet column label and returns the string. The mapping is a bijective base-26 numbering: 1 is A, 26 is Z, 27 is AA, 28 is AB, 52 is AZ, 53 is BA, 702 is ZZ, 703 is AAA. There is no zero digit and no leading-A padding because the scheme is bijective, not ordinary positional base 26. n must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad column'). The label is always uppercase ASCII letters. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function col_number(s) that converts a spreadsheet column label into its 1-based column index and returns the integer. It is the inverse of the bijective base-26 labeling: A is 1, Z is 26, AA is 27, AZ is 52, ZZ is 702, AAA is 703. s must be a str, must be non-empty, and must consist only of uppercase ASCII letters A through Z; an empty string, any lowercase letter, any digit, and any other character each -> ValueError('bad label'). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function luhn_valid(s) that checks a string of decimal digits against the Luhn checksum and returns a bool. s must be a str, must be non-empty, and must contain only ASCII decimal digits; a non-string, an empty string, or any non-ASCII-digit character each -> ValueError('bad number'). The Luhn rule: walking from the rightmost digit leftward, leave digits in odd positions (the rightmost is position one, counted as position zero here) as they are and double the digit in every second position; a doubled digit greater than nine has nine subtracted from it. Sum all the resulting digits; the string is valid when that sum is a multiple of ten. Return True when valid, False otherwise. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function isbn10_check(s) that validates an ISBN-10 string and returns a bool. s must be a str of exactly ten characters; a non-string or any other length -> ValueError('bad isbn'). The first nine characters must be ASCII decimal digits. The tenth character is the check symbol: it is either an ASCII decimal digit or an uppercase letter X, where X stands for the value ten; a lowercase x is not accepted, and an X in any of the first nine positions is not accepted. Any character that breaks these rules -> ValueError('bad isbn'). Compute the weighted sum where the first character is multiplied by ten, the second by nine, and so on down to the tenth character multiplied by one; the string is valid when that sum is a multiple of eleven. Return True when valid, False otherwise. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function days_in_month(year, month) that returns the number of days in a month of the proleptic Gregorian calendar. year must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad year'). month must be an int, must not be a bool, and must satisfy 1 <= month <= 12; otherwise -> ValueError('bad month'). April, June, September, and November have 30 days; the other non-February months have 31. February has 29 days in a leap year and 28 otherwise. A year is a leap year when it is divisible by four, except that years divisible by one hundred are not leap years unless they are also divisible by four hundred (so 1900 is common but 2000 is leap). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function ordinal_day(year, month, day) that returns the 1-based day-of-year ordinal of a proleptic Gregorian date, so January 1 is 1 and December 31 is 365 in a common year or 366 in a leap year. Validation runs in this order, each failure its own ValueError with exactly the message. year must be an int, not a bool, at least 1 -> 'bad year'. month must be an int, not a bool, in 1 through 12 -> 'bad month'. day must be an int, not a bool, at least 1, and at most the number of days that month actually has in that year (accounting for leap years, where a year is leap when divisible by four but not by one hundred unless also by four hundred) -> 'bad day'. So February 29 is valid only in a leap year. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function weekday_name(year, month, day) that returns the English weekday name of a proleptic Gregorian date, one of the strings Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Validate the date exactly as follows, each failure its own ValueError with exactly the message: year an int, not a bool, at least 1 -> 'bad year'; month an int, not a bool, in 1 through 12 -> 'bad month'; day an int, not a bool, at least 1 and at most the real length of that month in that year, with leap Februaries having 29 days under the usual divisible-by-four, except-hundreds, unless-four-hundreds rule -> 'bad day'. For reference January 1 of the year 2000 was a Saturday and January 1 of 1970 was a Thursday. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function days_between(d1, d2) that returns the signed number of days from d1 to d2 (that is, d2 minus d1) as an int, positive when d2 is later, zero when equal, negative when earlier. Each argument must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly three values (year, month, day), each an int and not a bool, forming a valid proleptic Gregorian date: year at least 1, month in 1 through 12, day at least 1 and at most the real length of that month in that year (leap Februaries have 29 days under the divisible-by-four, except-hundreds, unless-four-hundreds rule). Any violation in either argument -> ValueError('bad date'). Counting is by whole days: consecutive calendar days differ by one, and crossing a leap day counts. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function semver_compare(a, b) that compares two semantic version strings and returns -1 if a has lower precedence than b, 0 if they have equal precedence, and 1 if a is higher. Each version must be three dot-separated numeric identifiers major.minor.patch, each a run of ASCII digits with no leading zero (except a lone 0), optionally followed by a hyphen and a pre-release made of one or more dot-separated identifiers. A pre-release identifier is either all ASCII digits with no leading zero, or a run of ASCII letters, digits, and hyphens containing at least one non-digit. Any deviation, including build metadata, an empty identifier, or a non-string -> ValueError('bad version'). Precedence rules: compare major, then minor, then patch as integers; a version with a pre-release ranks lower than the otherwise-equal version without one; when both have pre-releases compare their identifiers left to right, where a purely numeric identifier ranks lower than a non-numeric one, two numeric identifiers compare as integers, two non-numeric identifiers compare by ASCII order, and if all shared identifiers are equal the one with more identifiers ranks higher. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function natural_compare(a, b) that compares two strings in natural (human) order and returns -1, 0, or 1. Both arguments must be strings; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Split each string into a sequence of maximal runs that alternate between runs of ASCII digits and runs of non-digit characters. Compare the two sequences run by run: if one run is a digit run and the aligned run is a non-digit run, the digit run compares as smaller; two digit runs compare first by integer value, and if the values are equal the run with fewer characters (fewer leading zeros) compares as smaller; two non-digit runs compare by ASCII order of their characters. If all aligned runs are equal but one sequence has more runs, the shorter sequence compares as smaller. Only equal-length sequences that match run for run give 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function percent_decode(s) that decodes a percent-encoded ASCII string and returns the decoded string. s must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). A percent sign introduces an escape and must be followed by exactly two hexadecimal digits (0 through 9 and a through f in either case); the two digits name a byte value. If a percent sign is not followed by two hexadecimal digits (including a percent sign at or near the end of the string) -> ValueError('bad escape'). If the named byte value is 128 or greater (outside 7-bit ASCII) -> ValueError('non-ascii byte'). Otherwise the byte becomes the character with that code point. A plus sign is a literal plus sign, NOT a space, in this decoder. Every other character is copied through unchanged. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function csv_quote(field) that encodes a single CSV field in the RFC 4180 style and returns the encoded string. field must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad field'). The field must be quoted if and only if it contains at least one of these four characters: a comma, a double quote, a carriage return, or a line feed. To quote a field, wrap the whole field in double quotes and double every double-quote character that appears inside it. A field with none of those four characters is returned exactly as-is, including when it contains spaces or is empty (the empty string returns the empty string, never a pair of quotes). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function round_half_even(num, den) that rounds the exact rational number num divided by den to the nearest integer using round-half-to-even (banker's rounding) and returns that int. Both arguments must be ints and not bools; otherwise -> ValueError('bad arg'). den must not be zero; otherwise -> ValueError('div by zero'). The sign of den is handled correctly, so the result of num over den has the usual mathematical sign regardless of which operand is negative. When the exact value is not a half-integer, round to the nearer integer. When it is exactly halfway between two integers, round to whichever of the two is even. So 1/2 rounds to 0, 3/2 rounds to 2, 5/2 rounds to 2, and -1/2 rounds to 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function reverse_bits(n, width) that reverses the order of the low `width` bits of a non-negative integer and returns the resulting integer. Both arguments must be ints and not bools; otherwise -> ValueError('bad arg'). width must be at least 1 and n must be at least 0; a width below 1 or a negative n -> ValueError('bad arg'). n must fit in width bits, meaning n must be strictly less than two to the power width; otherwise -> ValueError('overflow'). Treat n as exactly width bits (the most significant of those bits may be zero) and reverse their order, so the least significant bit becomes the most significant. For example with width 8 the value 1 becomes 128, and with width 4 the value binary 1010 becomes binary 0101. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function reduce_fraction(num, den) that reduces a fraction to lowest terms and returns it as a tuple (numerator, denominator). Both arguments must be ints and not bools; otherwise -> ValueError('bad arg'). den must not be zero; otherwise -> ValueError('div by zero'). Divide both parts by their greatest common divisor. The returned denominator is always strictly positive, so any negative sign is carried on the numerator (a fraction like 4 over -8 reduces to -1 over 2). A zero numerator always reduces to the tuple (0, 1) regardless of the denominator. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function top_k(items, k) that returns the k most frequent strings in a list, as a list of the strings themselves (not their counts). k must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad k'). Every element of items must be a str; any non-string element -> ValueError('bad item'). Rank the distinct strings by descending frequency, breaking ties by ascending lexicographic (ASCII) order of the string, and return the first k of that ranking. When k is 0 return the empty list. When k exceeds the number of distinct strings, return all distinct strings in ranked order (never pad and never repeat). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function uniq_counts(items) that collapses each maximal run of equal consecutive elements into a two-element list [value, run_length] and returns the list of those pairs, in order. items must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Only ADJACENT equal elements merge, so a value that reappears after a different value starts a fresh run. Two elements merge only when they are equal AND of the same type, so an integer 1 and the boolean True never merge into one run even though they compare equal. The empty list returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function eval_bool(expr) that evaluates a boolean expression string and returns a bool. expr must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad expr'). After removing all whitespace the expression is built from these single characters only: T for true, F for false, the operators for logical and, or, and not, and round parentheses for grouping. The and operator binds tighter than the or operator, and the not operator binds tightest of all and may stack. Evaluation is left to right within a precedence level. Any character outside the allowed set, any unbalanced parenthesis, any missing operand, and any leftover unparsed input each -> ValueError('bad expr'); in particular the empty string is invalid. Use the ampersand for and, the vertical bar for or, and the exclamation mark for not. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function glob_match(pattern, name) that reports whether a name matches a glob pattern and returns a bool. Both arguments must be strings; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). The pattern uses two wildcards: a star matches any run of zero or more characters, and a question mark matches exactly one character. Every other character is a literal that must match itself. The match is anchored: the pattern must match the ENTIRE name, not a prefix or a substring. There are no character classes or escaping. So a star followed by .txt matches any name ending in .txt including one where the star matches nothing, a question mark matches a single character but not zero characters, and an empty pattern matches only the empty name. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function sliding_windows(items, size, step) that returns the list of fixed-size sliding windows over a list. items must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). size must be an int, not a bool, at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad size'). step must be an int, not a bool, at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad step'). A window is a sublist of exactly `size` consecutive elements; windows start at index 0, then step, then two times step, and so on. Only FULL windows are produced: any trailing partial window that would run past the end of the list is dropped. If the list is shorter than one full window the result is the empty list. Each window is a new list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function summarize_ranges(nums) that summarizes a strictly increasing list of integers into a list of range strings. Every element must be an int and not a bool; any other element -> ValueError('bad item'). The list must be strictly increasing, so each element is greater than the one before; an element that is equal to or less than its predecessor -> ValueError('not sorted'). Walk the list and coalesce each maximal run of consecutive integers (each exactly one more than the last) into a single entry. A run of length one becomes the decimal string of that number; a longer run becomes the first number, then the two characters made of a hyphen and a greater-than sign, then the last number. The empty list returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function transpose(m) that returns the transpose of a rectangular matrix. m must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad matrix'). Each element of m is a row and must itself be a list; any row that is not a list -> ValueError('bad matrix'). All rows must have the same length; a row whose length differs from the first row's length -> ValueError('ragged'). The transpose swaps rows and columns, so the cell at row r and column c of the input becomes the cell at row c and column r of the output. A matrix with no rows, and a matrix whose rows are all empty, each transpose to the empty list. Cell values are copied as-is. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function json_escape(s) that returns the JSON-escaped form of a string WITHOUT surrounding quotes. s must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Apply exactly these replacements. A double quote becomes a backslash followed by a double quote. A backslash becomes two backslashes. A newline becomes a backslash followed by the letter n. A carriage return becomes a backslash followed by the letter r. A tab becomes a backslash followed by the letter t. A backspace (code point 8) becomes a backslash followed by the letter b. A form feed (code point 12) becomes a backslash followed by the letter f. Any other control character whose code point is below 32 becomes a six-character sequence: a backslash, the letter u, then exactly four lowercase hexadecimal digits of the code point. Every other character passes through unchanged. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function normalize_path(p) that normalizes an absolute Unix-style path and returns the canonical string. p must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad path'). The path must be absolute, meaning it starts with a forward slash; otherwise -> ValueError('not absolute'). Split on slashes and process segments left to right: an empty segment (from a repeated slash) and a single-dot segment are both discarded; a double-dot segment removes the most recent surviving segment, but at the root it has no effect and cannot rise above the root; any other segment is kept literally. Rebuild the path with single slashes and a single leading slash. Any trailing slash is dropped, except that the root itself normalizes to a lone slash. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function ipv4_to_int(s) that parses a strict dotted-quad IPv4 address and returns its 32-bit integer value. s must be a str consisting of exactly four parts separated by dots. Each part must be a run of ASCII decimal digits naming a value from 0 to 255, with no leading zero (except the single character 0), no sign, no spaces, and no empty part. Any violation, a non-string, or the wrong number of parts each -> ValueError('bad address'). The value is big-endian: the first part is the most significant byte, so 1.2.3.4 is 1 times 16777216 plus 2 times 65536 plus 3 times 256 plus 4, and 0.0.0.0 is 0 while 255.255.255.255 is 4294967295. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function multiset_diff(a, b) that returns the multiset difference a minus b as a sorted list of integers. a and b are lists; every element of both must be an int and not a bool, and any other element -> ValueError('bad item'). Treat each list as a multiset (a bag that counts repetitions). For every distinct value, its count in the result is its count in a minus its count in b, but never below zero, so a value that appears three times in a and once in b appears twice in the result, and a value with more copies in b than in a does not appear at all. The returned list is sorted in ascending order. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function parse_a1(ref) that parses a spreadsheet A1-style cell reference into a tuple (row, col) of 1-based integers. ref must be a non-empty str made of one or more uppercase ASCII letters (the column) immediately followed by one or more ASCII decimal digits (the row). The column letters use bijective base-26 numbering, so A is column 1, Z is 26, AA is 27, AB is 28. The row is a positive decimal integer with no leading zero, so the smallest row is 1. Anything else, including a non-string, an empty string, a missing letter part, a missing digit part, a lowercase letter, a leading zero in the row, a zero row, or letters appearing after digits, each -> ValueError('bad ref'). The returned tuple lists the row first and the column second. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function has_cycle(nxt) that detects whether following links from node 0 enters a cycle, returning a bool. nxt is a list where nxt[i] is the index of the node that node i points to, or -1 to mean it points to nothing. Every element must be an int and not a bool, and must be either -1 or a valid index from 0 up to len(nxt) minus 1; any other value -> ValueError('bad link'). Starting at node 0, repeatedly move to the node named by the current node's link. If a -1 link is reached the traversal ends with no cycle. If a node is visited a second time, the traversal is in a cycle. The empty list has no node 0 to start from and returns False. A node whose link points to itself is a cycle. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function tour_length(points) that returns the total Manhattan distance of visiting a sequence of grid points in order, as an int. points is a list; each element must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly two values (x, y), each an int and not a bool; any element that is not such a tuple, or whose coordinates are not ints or are bools, -> ValueError('bad point'). The Manhattan distance between two points is the absolute difference of their x coordinates plus the absolute difference of their y coordinates. The tour length is the sum of the distances between each consecutive pair of points in the list. A list with fewer than two points has length 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function parse_kv(s) that parses a semicolon-separated list of key-value assignments into a list of (key, value) tuples in order. s must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). The empty string returns the empty list. Otherwise split on semicolons; each item must contain exactly one equals sign that separates a non-empty key from a value. The key must be non-empty and consist only of ASCII letters, ASCII digits, and underscores; the value is the remainder and may be empty but must not contain a further equals sign. A duplicate key (one already seen earlier in the same string) -> ValueError('duplicate key'). Any malformed item (no equals sign, an empty key, a bad key character, a second equals sign, or an empty item from a stray semicolon) -> ValueError('bad item'). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function rotate(items, k) that returns a NEW list equal to items rotated to the right by k positions, without mutating the input. items must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). k must be an int and not a bool; otherwise -> ValueError('bad shift'). A right rotation by k moves the last k elements to the front while preserving order, so rotating by 1 moves the final element to position 0. k is taken modulo the length, so a k equal to or larger than the length wraps around, and a negative k rotates to the left instead. Rotating the empty list gives the empty list. The input list object must be left unchanged. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function group_anagrams(words) that groups words that are anagrams of one another and returns a list of groups. words is a list; every element must be a str, and any non-string element -> ValueError('bad item'). Two words are anagrams when they contain exactly the same multiset of characters; the comparison is case sensitive, so an uppercase and lowercase letter are different characters. Within each group the words are sorted in ascending ASCII order, and a word that appears more than once appears that many times in its group. The groups themselves are ordered by the ascending ASCII order of their first (smallest) word. The empty list returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function stock_spans(prices) that returns the list of stock spans for a sequence of daily prices. Each element of prices must be an int or a float but not a bool; any other element -> ValueError('bad price'). The span for a given day is the number of consecutive days ending at that day (including the day itself) on which the price was less than or equal to that day's price, walking backward and stopping at the first earlier day with a strictly greater price. So the span is always at least 1, equals the day index plus 1 when all earlier prices are less than or equal to today's, and equal prices extend the span. The empty list returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function perm_rank(perm) that returns the 0-based rank of a permutation in the lexicographic ordering of all permutations of 0..n-1. perm must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Every element must be an int and not a bool; any other element -> ValueError('bad element'). The list must contain every integer from 0 to len(perm)-1 exactly once; a duplicate, a missing value, or an out-of-range value -> ValueError('not a permutation'). Checks run in that order: the list check, then the element type check across all elements, then the permutation check. Among the n! permutations of 0..n-1 listed in ascending lexicographic order, return the position of perm counting from 0, so [0, 1, ..., n-1] has rank 0 and the fully descending permutation has rank n! - 1. The empty list is the unique permutation of nothing and has rank 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function gray_rank(bits) that returns the 0-based position of a codeword in the reflected binary Gray code sequence, as an int. bits must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad code'). It must be non-empty and every character must be the digit 0 or the digit 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad code'). The width n is the length of bits, and the n-bit sequence lists, for each index i from 0 to 2**n - 1, the value i xor (i right-shifted by one bit), printed as exactly n binary digits with the most significant bit first. gray_rank inverts that listing: given the printed codeword it returns the index i at which the codeword appears. So in the 3-bit sequence '000' is at index 0, '001' at 1, '011' at 2, '010' at 3, '110' at 4, '111' at 5, '101' at 6, and '100' at 7. Leading zeros only widen the printing and never change the index, so '0011' in the 4-bit sequence is also at index 2. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function kth_combination(n, k, r) that returns the combination at rank r in the lexicographic listing of all k-element combinations of the integers 0..n-1, as a sorted list. n must be an int, not a bool, and at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad n'). k must be an int, not a bool, and satisfy 0 <= k <= n; otherwise -> ValueError('bad k'). r must be an int, not a bool, and satisfy 0 <= r < C(n, k) where C is the binomial coefficient; otherwise -> ValueError('bad rank'). Checks run in that order: n first, then k, then r. Each combination is written as its ascending sorted list of members, and the combinations are listed in ascending lexicographic order of those lists, so for n = 4 and k = 2 the listing is [0,1], [0,2], [0,3], [1,2], [1,3], [2,3] and rank 3 is [1,2]. When k is 0 the only combination is the empty list at rank 0, so any other rank -> ValueError('bad rank'). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function look_and_say(seed, steps) that applies the look-and-say expansion a fixed number of times and returns the resulting string. seed must be a str, non-empty, and every character must be an ASCII decimal digit; otherwise -> ValueError('bad seed'). steps must be an int, not a bool, and at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad steps'). Seed validation happens before steps validation. One step reads the current string left to right as maximal runs of equal digits and writes, for each run, the run length followed by the digit, so '3993' becomes '132913' and '1' becomes '11'. Reading is strict: if any run in the string being read is longer than 9 characters its length would not be a single digit, so raise ValueError('run overflow'). That check applies only when a step actually reads the string: with steps equal to 0 the seed is returned unchanged even if it contains a run longer than 9. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function longest_digit_run(n) that locates the longest run of equal consecutive digits in the decimal representation of a non-negative integer. n must be an int, not a bool, and at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad number'). Use the ordinary base-10 representation with no sign and no leading zeros; 0 is the single digit 0. A run is a maximal block of equal consecutive digits, meaning it cannot be extended on either side. Return a tuple of exactly three ints (start, length, digit): the 0-based index of the run's first digit counted from the most significant digit, the run's length, and the digit's numeric value. When several runs share the maximal length, return the leftmost one (the smallest start). A single-digit number returns (0, 1, that digit). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function collatz_trace(n, limit) that returns the full Collatz trajectory of n as a list, computed under a strict step budget. n must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad start'). limit must be an int, not a bool, and at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad limit'). n is validated before limit. One step maps an even value to value // 2 and an odd value to 3 * value + 1. The trace starts with n itself and appends the value after each step, stopping once the value 1 has been appended; if n is already 1 the trace is [1] with zero steps taken, whatever the limit. Steps are transitions, so the trace always has exactly one more element than the number of steps taken. If reaching 1 would require MORE than limit steps, raise RuntimeError('limit exceeded') instead of returning; reaching 1 in exactly limit steps succeeds. The two failure kinds are distinct: validation failures are ValueError and budget exhaustion is RuntimeError. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function knight_moves(n, start, goal) that returns the minimum number of chess-knight moves needed to travel from start to goal on an n-by-n board, or -1 when the goal is unreachable. n must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad board'). start and goal must each be EXACTLY a tuple (not a list or any other sequence) of exactly two values (row, col), each an int and not a bool, each from 0 to n-1 inclusive; any violation -> ValueError('bad cell'). Validate n first, then start, then goal. A knight move jumps two squares along one axis and one square along the perpendicular axis, in any of the eight combinations; only the landing square must lie on the board. When start equals goal the answer is 0, even on a 1-by-1 board. On a board too small for any knight move every other square is unreachable, so the answer is -1. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function path_steps(grid) that returns the length in moves of the shortest path through a rectangular grid, or -1 when no path exists. grid must be a list with at least one row, and every row must be a list with at least one cell; otherwise -> ValueError('bad grid'). Every row must have the same length as the first row; otherwise -> ValueError('ragged'). Every cell must be the int 0 (open floor) or the int 1 (wall) and must not be a bool; otherwise -> ValueError('bad cell'). Perform those three checks in that order. The path starts at the top-left cell (row 0, column 0) and ends at the bottom-right cell, moving one cell up, down, left, or right at a time and only through open cells. Return the number of moves in the shortest such path. When the start cell or the goal cell is a wall, or no route exists, return -1. A 1-by-1 grid whose only cell is open returns 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function component_count(n, edges) that returns the number of connected components of an undirected graph whose nodes are numbered 0 to n-1. n must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad n'). edges must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad edges'). Every edge must be EXACTLY a tuple (not a list or any other sequence) of exactly two values, each an int and not a bool, each from 0 to n-1 inclusive; any violation -> ValueError('bad edge'). Validate n, then the edges container, then every edge, all before any counting. A self-loop edge and a duplicate edge are both legal and change nothing beyond connecting what they connect. With no edges the answer is n, and when n is 0 the answer is 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function is_bipartite(adj) that reports whether an undirected graph is bipartite, returning a bool. adj is an adjacency list: adj[i] is the list of neighbors of node i. adj must be a list and every entry of adj must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad adjacency'). Every neighbor must be an int, not a bool, from 0 to len(adj)-1 inclusive; otherwise -> ValueError('bad neighbor'). The listing must be symmetric: whenever j appears in adj[i], i must also appear in adj[j]; otherwise -> ValueError('not symmetric'). Run those three validations in that order, finishing each over the whole structure before starting the next, and only then decide bipartiteness. Duplicate neighbor entries are legal. The graph is bipartite when its nodes can be split into two sets so that every edge joins the two sets; the graph may be disconnected and every component must qualify. A self-loop (a node listed among its own neighbors) passes the symmetry check on its own but makes the graph NOT bipartite. The empty list is bipartite. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function portal_moves(n, portals, start, goal) that returns the minimum number of moves to travel between two cells of a one-dimensional board with one-way teleporters. The board has n cells numbered 0 to n-1. n must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad n'). start and goal must each be an int, not a bool, from 0 to n-1 inclusive; otherwise -> ValueError('bad cell'); check start before goal. portals must be a list, and every element must be EXACTLY a tuple (not a list) of exactly two values (entry, exit), each an int and not a bool, each from 0 to n-1 inclusive; any violation -> ValueError('bad portal'). If two portals share the same entry cell, including the same pair listed twice, -> ValueError('duplicate portal'). Validate n first, then start and goal, then the portals in order. One move goes from cell i to cell i-1 (when i-1 is at least 0), to cell i+1 (when i+1 is at most n-1), or, when i is a portal entry, to that portal's exit. Every move costs exactly 1 and portals are one-way: standing on an exit does not allow jumping back. When start equals goal the answer is 0. The goal is always reachable by unit steps, so the function always returns an int. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function spread_radius(grid) that computes how many steps a signal needs to spread from its sources to cover a grid. grid must be a list with at least one row, and every row must be a str with at least one character; otherwise -> ValueError('bad grid'). Every row must have the same length as the first row; otherwise -> ValueError('ragged'). Every character must be one of: the uppercase letter S (a source), the period (open floor), or the hash sign (a wall); otherwise -> ValueError('bad cell'). The grid must contain at least one S; otherwise -> ValueError('no source'). Perform those four checks in that order. The signal starts at every source at time 0 and each step spreads one cell up, down, left, and right into cells that are not walls. Return the largest number of steps needed for the signal to first reach an open-floor cell, that is, the maximum over all open cells of the distance to the nearest source. When some open cell can never be reached return -1. When the grid has no open-floor cells at all return 0. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function lru_trace(capacity, ops) that simulates an LRU cache and returns the list of results of the get operations, in order. capacity must be an int, must not be a bool, and must be at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad capacity'). Each element of ops must be EXACTLY a tuple of the form ('get', key) with exactly two items or ('put', key, value) with exactly three items; any other element (wrong type, wrong length, or an unknown first item) -> ValueError('bad op'), raised when that element is reached in left-to-right processing. A get of a present key appends its value to the result list and makes that key the most recently used. A get of a missing key appends None and leaves the recency order unchanged. A put of an existing key replaces its value and makes it the most recently used, never evicting. A put of a new key when the cache already holds capacity keys first evicts the least recently used key, then inserts. Only get operations append to the returned list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function min_stack(ops) that simulates a stack with minimum tracking and returns the list of outputs, in order. ops must be a list; otherwise -> ValueError('bad ops'). Each element must be EXACTLY one of these tuples: ('push', v) with exactly two items where v is an int and not a bool; ('pop',), ('top',), or ('min',), each with exactly one item. Any other element -> ValueError('bad op'), raised when that element is reached in left-to-right processing. push adds v to the top of the stack and produces no output. pop removes the top value and appends it to the output list. top appends the top value without removing it. min appends the smallest value currently on the stack, leaving the stack unchanged. pop, top, and min on an empty stack each -> ValueError('empty stack'). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function ring_buffer(capacity, ops) that simulates a circular buffer that overwrites its oldest element when full, and returns the list of outputs, in order. capacity must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1; otherwise -> ValueError('bad capacity'). Each element of ops must be EXACTLY a tuple ('write', v) with exactly two items, or ('read',) or ('peek',) with exactly one item; anything else -> ValueError('bad op'), raised when that element is reached in left-to-right processing. write appends v at the newest end; when the buffer already holds capacity elements the oldest element is dropped to make room, and write appends the dropped element to the output list, otherwise write appends None. read removes the oldest element and appends it to the output list. peek appends the oldest element without removing it. read and peek on an empty buffer each -> ValueError('buffer empty'). Every operation appends exactly one entry to the output list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function k_smallest(records, k) that returns the names of the k lowest-scoring records. Validate k first: it must be an int, not a bool, and at least 0; otherwise -> ValueError('bad k'). Then scan records left to right: each element must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly two items (name, score) where name is a str and score is an int and not a bool; any other element -> ValueError('bad record'). A name equal to the name of an earlier record -> ValueError('duplicate name'). Rank the records by ascending score, breaking ties by ascending lexicographic (ASCII) order of name, and return a list of just the names of the first k records in that ranking. When k is 0 return the empty list; when k exceeds the number of records return all names in ranked order (never pad and never repeat). Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function bank_ledger(ops) that folds a list of banking operations over a balance that starts at 0 and returns the list of balances after each operation, in order. Each element of ops must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly two items ('deposit', amount) or ('withdraw', amount); any other element -> ValueError('bad op'), raised when that element is reached in left-to-right processing. The op-shape check happens first; then amount must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1, otherwise -> ValueError('bad amount'). deposit adds amount to the balance. withdraw subtracts amount, but when amount exceeds the current balance it raises ValueError with EXACTLY the message 'insufficient funds: need N have B' where N is the decimal amount and B is the decimal current balance (for example withdrawing 50 from a balance of 30 raises ValueError('insufficient funds: need 50 have 30')). Withdrawing an amount exactly equal to the balance is allowed and leaves 0. After each successful operation the new balance is appended to the returned list. The empty list returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function reserve_trace(stock, ops) that folds inventory reservation operations and returns the final reservations. stock must be a dict whose every key is a str and whose every value is an int, not a bool, and at least 0; any violation -> ValueError('bad stock'), and the input dict must never be mutated. Each element of ops must be EXACTLY a tuple of exactly three items ('reserve', item, qty) or ('cancel', item, qty); any other element -> ValueError('bad op'). Per element, in this order: the shape check above; then qty must be an int, not a bool, and at least 1, otherwise -> ValueError('bad qty'); then item must be a key of stock, otherwise -> ValueError('unknown item'). reserve increases the item's reserved count by qty, but when qty exceeds the item's available count (its stock value minus its current reserved count) it raises ValueError with EXACTLY the message 'not enough ' followed by the item name. cancel decreases the item's reserved count by qty; when qty exceeds the current reserved count -> ValueError('over-cancel'). Reserving exactly the available count and cancelling exactly the reserved count are both allowed. Return a list of (item, reserved) tuples for every item whose final reserved count is greater than 0, sorted by ascending item name. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function split_url(url) that splits a URL string into a tuple (scheme, host, port, path, query). url must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad url'). The scheme is everything before the FIRST occurrence of the three-character separator colon slash slash; if that separator does not appear anywhere -> ValueError('no scheme'). The scheme must be non-empty, its first character must be a lowercase ASCII letter, and every following character must be a lowercase ASCII letter, an ASCII digit, a plus sign, a hyphen, or a dot; otherwise -> ValueError('bad scheme'). After the separator, the authority runs up to the first slash or question mark (or the end of the string). Within the authority, an optional port is introduced by the first colon; the part before that colon is the host. The host must be non-empty and contain only lowercase ASCII letters, ASCII digits, hyphens, and dots; otherwise -> ValueError('bad host'). When a colon is present, the port text must be one or more ASCII digits with no leading zero (a lone 0 is allowed) and its value must be at most 65535; anything else, including an empty port or a second colon in the authority, -> ValueError('bad port'). The port element of the tuple is that value as an int, or None when there is no colon. The path is the slash that ends the authority plus everything up to the first question mark; when the authority is followed by no slash the path is the single character /. The query is everything after the FIRST question mark (later question marks stay inside the query); it is the empty string for a trailing question mark and None when there is no question mark at all. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function qp_decode(s) that decodes a quoted-printable style string and returns the decoded str. s must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Scan left to right. An equals sign starts an escape and is never emitted literally. An equals sign followed by exactly two uppercase hexadecimal digits (0-9 and A-F only) decodes to the single character whose code point is that two-digit hex value. An equals sign followed immediately by a line feed, or by a carriage return then a line feed, is a soft line break: the equals sign and that line ending are deleted and contribute nothing to the output. Any other use of the equals sign, including lowercase hex digits, fewer than two characters remaining before the end of the string, a carriage return not followed by a line feed, or any non-hex character in the two positions after the equals sign, raises ValueError('bad escape'). Every character other than the equals sign, including bare line feeds not preceded by an equals sign, passes through unchanged. The empty string decodes to the empty string. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function parse_ini(text) that parses a sectioned INI document into a dict mapping each section name to a dict of its keys to values. text must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). Split the text on line feeds and process each line after stripping leading and trailing spaces and tabs. A stripped line that is empty, or whose first character is a semicolon or a hash, is skipped as blank or comment. A stripped line whose first character is an opening square bracket is a section header: it must also end with a closing square bracket, and the name between the brackets must be non-empty and made only of ASCII letters, ASCII digits, and underscores; any violation -> ValueError('bad section'). A section name that has already appeared -> ValueError('duplicate section'); a new section starts as an empty dict. Every other line must be a key-value assignment containing an equals sign: the key is the text before the FIRST equals sign and the value is everything after it, each stripped of surrounding spaces and tabs; the value may be empty and may contain further equals signs. The key must be non-empty and made only of ASCII letters, ASCII digits, and underscores; a line with no equals sign, or a bad key, -> ValueError('bad line'). A well-formed assignment that appears before any section header -> ValueError('no section'). A key repeated inside the same section -> ValueError('duplicate key'); the same key in different sections is allowed. The empty document returns the empty dict. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function diff_ops(a, b) that computes a line diff between two lists of strings and returns a list of (tag, items) tuples, where tag is one of the strings 'equal', 'delete', 'insert' and items is a list of consecutive elements sharing that tag. a and b must both be lists and every element of both must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). The diff must be MINIMAL: it deletes elements of a and inserts elements of b around an unchanged longest common subsequence, so the total number of deleted plus inserted elements is as small as possible. Among all minimal diffs, produce exactly this one: walk both lists from the front; when the current element of a equals the current element of b, pair them as an 'equal' and advance both; when they differ, emit the current element of a as a 'delete' whenever doing so still permits a minimal diff for the remainders, and only otherwise emit the current element of b as an 'insert'; when one list is exhausted the remainder of the other is all deletes or all inserts. This rule places a delete before an insert whenever both choices would preserve minimality. Consecutive operations with the same tag are coalesced into a single tuple whose items list holds those elements in order. Two empty lists produce the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function fletcher16(data) that computes the Fletcher-16 checksum and returns it as an int. data may be a str or a list; anything else -> ValueError('bad input'). When data is a str, every character must have a code point of at most 127 (7-bit ASCII); a character beyond that -> ValueError('bad char'); the byte sequence is the characters' code points in order. When data is a list, every element must be an int, must not be a bool, and must lie in the range 0 to 255 inclusive; any other element -> ValueError('bad byte'). The checksum uses two running sums that both start at 0: for each byte in order, first add the byte to the first sum modulo 255, then add the (updated) first sum to the second sum modulo 255. The result is the second sum times 256 plus the first sum. Empty input (empty string or empty list) gives 0. For example, the string 'abcde' gives 51440. Output ONLY the function definition.

Write a Python function outline_number(lines) that numbers markdown-style headers hierarchically. lines must be a list and every element must be a str; otherwise -> ValueError('bad input'). A line is a header candidate exactly when its FIRST character is a hash. A valid header is 1 to 6 hashes, then exactly one space, then a non-empty title whose first character is not a space; a header candidate that breaks any of those rules (7 or more hashes, no space right after the hashes, an empty title, or a title starting with a space) -> ValueError('bad header'). The title itself may contain further hashes and spaces. The header's level is its number of leading hashes. Lines that do not start with a hash are ignored. The first header must be level 1, and every header may be at most one level deeper than the header before it (any number of levels shallower is fine); a violation -> ValueError('bad nesting'). Number the headers with one counter per level: a header of level k increments the level-k counter and resets all deeper counters, and its output string is the counters for levels 1 through k joined with single dots, then a single space, then the title. So the first level-1 header is '1 Title', its first level-2 child is '1.1 Sub', and a later second level-1 header is '2 Next'. Return the list of these numbered strings in order; a list with no headers returns the empty list. Output ONLY the function definition.
